items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Memory is now generally available
items.summary:
Today, AWS announced the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new serverless capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions, so agents can recall prior decisions, earlier interactions, and user preferences without replaying the full conversation history to the model. Customers can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems.

OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It manages the full memory lifecycle, including extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation (adding, updating, or skipping memories as new information arrives), and retrieval using keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Customers control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for each memory store, with actor and session scoping, and can set expiration periods for events and memories. Because it is serverless, there are no clusters to provision, instance types to choose, or indexes to create, and capacity for extraction and search scales automatically.

Amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Regions. For pricing details about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, visit the pricing page.

To learn more about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, see the technical documentation and launch blog. You can get started by visiting the technical launch blog that details how to add persistent memory to your agents with Amazon OpenSearch Memory.

items.title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for AWS Glue ETL
items.summary:
AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and reasoning behind each suggestion. You can use the agent on any completed job run from the AWS Glue console, or from your own tools through the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. When cost and performance trade off, the agent improves the metric you chose while keeping any regression of the other within defined limits. The engine also checks best practices such as platform-level improvements like upgrading to a newer AWS Glue version or using AWS Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the area it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. All access is authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR and AWS Glue and the blog post - Introducing the Apache Spark optimization agent for Amazon EMR Serverless and AWS Glue ETL.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports cross-Region inference routing
items.summary:
Today, Amazon SageMaker AI announces cross-Region inference routing, which helps keep inference applications available when a region runs short of capacity by sending requests to endpoints deployed in other AWS Regions and AWS accounts. Models served on accelerated instances can reach capacity limits in a single Region, and an unhealthy endpoint can lead to throttling and errors for end users. Previously, teams had to build and maintain their own routing, health checks, and retry logic across Regions.

With cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, developers create an inference router, register the real-time endpoints, asynchronous endpoints, and inference components they already run, and point their applications at the router. The router prefers endpoints in its own Region, shifts new requests to healthy destinations in other Regions as errors rise, and returns traffic gradually after the local endpoint recovers. Existing endpoints, models, and containers do not change. Endpoint owners stay in control: an endpoint policy determines which routers in other accounts can use an endpoint, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap reserves capacity for the endpoint’s local callers. Each real-time response identifies the endpoint that served the request and the reason, and router metrics in Amazon CloudWatch show where traffic went.

Cross-Region inference routing is available for real-time inference in 32 commercial AWS Regions, and for asynchronous inference in 25 Regions. There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing. Customers pay standard SageMaker AI pricing for the endpoints that serve requests and standard Amazon CloudWatch rates for router metrics. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and SageMaker AI Deployment page.

items.title: AWS announces ExtendDB 1.0
items.summary:
Today, Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced version 1.0 of ExtendDB, the first release of the open source Amazon DynamoDB-compatible adapter for production use. ExtendDB is fully compatible with the DynamoDB API and runs on a database backend that you choose, so developers and infrastructure teams can run DynamoDB workloads in on-premises data centers, in private or public clouds, and at the edge without rewriting application code.

ExtendDB 1.0 supports four storage backends, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Cassandra, and MongoDB. For local development and continuous integration (CI), the extenddb-dev container image and the @extenddb/dev npm package run a DynamoDB-compatible endpoint over SQLite, so you don’t have to set up an external database.

ExtendDB is maintained by AWS, released under the Apache 2.0 license, and developed in the open on GitHub. To learn more, see the ExtendDB project page. To get started or contribute, visit the GitHub repository.

items.title: AWS Transform custom now supports cross-account sharing of transformation definitions
items.summary:
AWS Transform custom now enables you to share transformation definitions (TDs) and their associated lessons across AWS accounts, organizational units (OUs), or your entire organization in AWS Organizations through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). AWS Transform custom is a capability of AWS Transform that performs transformations across your technology stack, including API and framework upgrades, migrations, and language translations.

With this launch, you can share TDs as live resources rather than static copies, so consumers run the owner's latest published version by default while the owner maintains full control. As the TD owner, you select from four managed permissions ranging from execute-only (the default) to permissions that allow consumers to use your lessons, contribute lessons back to you, or download the TD. Lessons flow back to the owner only when the permission allows it and the consumer opts in.

This capability is particularly valuable for platform engineering teams and AWS Partners who need to deploy standardized transformations across multiple accounts. A central team can create a TD once and share it organization-wide.

This feature is available via the AWS Transform CLI and AWS RAM in US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Canada (Central) Regions. To learn more, visit the AWS Transform User Guide.

items.title: Amazon CloudFront standard logging now supports CMCD and additional log fields
items.summary:
Amazon CloudFront standard logging now supports additional access log fields that were previously available only in CloudFront real-time logs. You can now include these fields in your standard logs and deliver them to Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, or Amazon Data Firehose, without setting up an additional data stream for real-time logs.

The new fields include the IP address of the CloudFront server that handled the request, identifiers that separate traffic on a primary distribution from traffic on a staging distribution, and a media quality confidence score. They also include Common Media Client Data (CMCD) fields, which video players send with each request to report details like bitrate, buffer length, and playback session ID. Streaming teams can use these fields to match playback problems that viewers see with CloudFront delivery data, which makes troubleshooting faster.

These fields are available in all CloudFront edge locations, and standard logging pricing applies. To learn more, see Standard logging page in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon CloudFront Announces WebSocket and gRPC Support for Origin Mutual TLS
items.summary:
Amazon CloudFront (CF) now supports WebSocket and gRPC traffic to application origins in AWS regions, with mutual TLS authentication between CF and the application origin (origin mTLS). Customers can now use TLS certificates to authenticate requests from CloudFront while setting up WebSocket or gRPC connections to their origins. Origin mTLS protects internet facing applications that need persistent, bidirectional or streaming connections, such as chat platforms, collaborative editing tools or live dashboards from unauthenticated requests.

Previously, customers serving WebSocket or gRPC traffic through CloudFront had to use shared secrets or IP allow-lists to identify requests originating from CloudFront. This was operationally complex and did not provide strong authentication. With Origin mTLS, customers can use one TLS based authentication for HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC traffic to an application origin. This works with application origins within AWS such as Application Load Balancer and API Gateway, on-premises origins, and origins hosted outside AWS.

There is no additional charge for origin mTLS, and it is available with pay-as-you-go pricing and in the Business and Premium flat-rate pricing plans. To learn more, visit the CloudFront origin mutual TLS documentation.

items.title: AWS Lambda adds support for GPU instances on Lambda Managed Instances
items.summary:
AWS Lambda now supports GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances using EC2 G-series instances. You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads including AI inference, media processing, 3D rendering, scientific computing, and financial simulations on Lambda without managing GPU drivers, frameworks, or scaling. Lambda runs multiple invocations concurrently in each execution environment and scales responsively based on GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency to keep your GPUs busy and reduce costs. GPU-accelerated functions integrate with the same 200+ AWS event sources as other Event Functions, so you can add GPU compute as another step in your serverless application.

Running GPU workloads today requires customers to provision hardware, manage driver and framework dependencies, and build custom scaling and capacity management. With this launch, you can go from code to a running GPU workload in minutes. Lambda provides GPU base images preconfigured with frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch. You can run workloads with large artifacts using container images and NVMe ephemeral storage of up to 32 GB each. To reduce startup time, Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading and streaming artifacts directly from Amazon S3. For resilience, you can select G-series instance types from multiple generations in the allowed instance types for your capacity provider. Lambda provisions instances from the newest generation that meets your function requirements and falls back to older generations when capacity is unavailable.

GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances and EC2 G-series instances are available. You can configure GPU-accelerated functions using the AWS Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use this feature through coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex by installing the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. You pay the EC2 On-Demand price (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply) for your instance, plus a 9.75% Lambda management fee and $0.20 per million requests. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda Pricing.

items.title: Amazon RDS for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13
items.summary:
Starting today, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13, the latest minor released by community MySQL. We recommend upgrading to the newer minor versions to accept fixes for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of MySQL and to benefit from bug fixes, performance improvements, and new functionality added by the MySQL community. Learn more about the enhancements in RDS for MySQL 8.4.13 in the Amazon RDS user guide and MySQL 8.4.13 release notes.

You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate upgrades across your instances in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS User Guide. This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for MySQL is available.

Amazon RDS for MySQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale MySQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

items.title: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery
items.summary:
Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery (PITR), so you can restore the user data in a user pool to an earlier time. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices. Previously, you had to build and maintain your own export and restore process, and restored users received new identifiers and had to reset their passwords.

With PITR, you choose a recovery point, preview how many users, groups, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys the recovery will create, update, or delete, and then start or cancel the recovery. Recovered users keep their identifiers, passwords, MFA settings, and passkeys, so they can sign in without resetting their credentials. For example, if a script deletes or modifies users by mistake, you can restore the user data to the moment before it ran.

PITR is enabled automatically for user pools on the Essentials and Plus feature plans at no additional charge. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. You can initiate and manage a recovery using the AWS Management Console, the Amazon Cognito API, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. PITR is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Point-in-time recovery in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon RDS for MySQL now supports MySQL major version 9.7
items.summary:
Starting today, Amazon RDS for MySQL supports MySQL major version 9.7, the latest Long-Term Support release from MySQL community. Amazon RDS for MySQL 9.7 launches with community MySQL 9.7.4. This launch introduces support for the Replication Applier Metrics component, JSON Duality Views, and Hypergraph Optimizer.  

The Replication Applier Metrics help you diagnose replication lag by adding two Performance Schema tables that report per-channel applier backlog, throughput, and wait statistics, along with each worker's progress on its current transaction. JSON Duality Views let applications read and write the same relational tables as JSON documents. The Hypergraph Optimizer is an opt-in query optimizer that can improve execution plans for complex, multi-join queries. For more details, refer to the MySQL 9.7.4 release notes and the Amazon RDS for MySQL release notes.

You can upgrade your database using Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments, in-place upgrade, or restore from a snapshot. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS User Guide. This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for MySQL is available. Learn more about pricing details at Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing.

Amazon RDS for MySQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale MySQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

items.title: Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes reduces price for large hosts
items.summary:
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Hybrid Nodes now has lower pricing for large nodes, capping the billed vCPU per node at 32 vCPU, so you are no longer charged for vCPUs above that per node threshold. Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes lets you use your existing on-premises and edge infrastructure as nodes in Amazon EKS clusters. You can now use your largest servers, including those with GPUs, with Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes at lower cost.

With this change, the Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes cost of a large server no longer grows with its vCPU count. At the first pricing tier, a 64 vCPU node now costs 50% less than before, and a 256 vCPU node costs 88% less, as both are now billed only for 32 vCPUs. This makes Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes more cost-effective for large bare-metal and GPU servers running compute-intensive workloads, such as AI/ML training and inference, that must stay on-premises for data residency, latency, or regulatory reasons. The pricing change applies automatically to all new hybrid nodes. For the new pricing to take effect for existing hybrid nodes attached to clusters, delete and reattach them. Nodes with 32 vCPUs or fewer are still billed for their actual vCPUs, and existing tiered pricing still applies, so your effective rate falls as monthly usage grows.

The new pricing is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes is available. To learn more about getting started and updated pricing details, visit the Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes documentation and Amazon EKS pricing page.

items.title: Amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls
items.summary:
Amazon CloudFront Functions can now make network calls and act on the response during a request. CloudFront Functions runs lightweight JavaScript at CloudFront edge locations to customize requests and responses. Previously, if your logic depended on data from another service, you had to use Lambda@Edge or move that logic to your origin. Now your functions can use real-time data to personalize, authenticate, or route requests at the edge, close to your viewers.

With the new cf.fetch() method, your functions can call your API endpoints and use the response to decide how to handle each request. For example, you can check an AI agent's permissions and usage budget so that only authorized requests reach your API or MCP server, or send request signals to a security or fraud detection service to block or challenge bad traffic. With cf.beacon(), you can send analytics events in the background without slowing down viewers, even for content served from cache. Both methods take advantage of the origin settings already on your distribution, including origin access control (OAC), VPC origins, and connection reuse.

Network calls are available at all CloudFront edge locations. They cost $0.10 per million calls, on top of CloudFront Functions invocation charges, and are included at no additional cost in the Pro plan and above in CloudFront flat-rate plans. To learn more, see Helper methods for network calls in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide and Amazon CloudFront pricing.

items.title: Amazon RDS now supports fast storage volume initialization
items.summary:
Amazon RDS now initializes storage volumes faster when you perform a point-in-time restore (PITR), create a read replica, or convert a Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ. Each of these operations creates storage volumes from a snapshot, and the data blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 before you can access them. With fast storage volume initialization, you get a fully performant DB instance in a predictable amount of time.

Previously, the initialization rate varied with your workload and with which blocks were accessed. As there was no dedicated bandwidth, so you could see increased I/O latency and had no way to tell when an instance would reach full performance. Now, each database instance is initialized at up to 4 TiB per hour, across every gp3 and io2 storage volume attached to the instance. If concurrent initialization across your account exceeds the available bandwidth, the remaining blocks initialize on a best-effort basis, so initialization is never slower than today. Your DB instance stays available and usable while initialization runs.

Fast storage volume initialization is enabled by default and no action is required. To follow progress, use the StorageOperationStatus and StorageOperationPercentProgress fields in the Amazon RDS console, the DescribeDBInstances API, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs.

This capability is available at no additional cost for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, RDS for Db2, RDS for Microsoft SQL Server, and RDS for Oracle, in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Amazon RDS storage in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

items.title: AWS Clean Rooms supports writing PySpark job results to intermediate tables
items.summary:
AWS Clean Rooms now supports intermediate tables for PySpark jobs, offering increased flexibility for organizations running complex, multi-step analytical workflows with their partners. With this launch, customers can write the results of a PySpark job to an intermediate table for reuse in subsequent analyses. For example, a measurement vendor can perform feature engineering with PySpark, then use those results as input into an ML model training job to identify new high-value customers to inform audience targeting and bid optimization for their campaigns.  

AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms.

items.title: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes, giving platform teams centralized control over runtime contents and updates
items.summary:
AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes for Lambda Event Functions (formerly Lambda functions). Customer-managed runtimes are a standalone resource type that fully decouples runtime management from function deployment. Platform teams gain centralized control over the runtime contents, updates, access, and lifecycle, including the ability to push updates to shared components without per-function redeployments. Application teams consume the runtime from their functions in the same way as a Lambda-managed runtime, preserving their familiar developer experience.

Many organizations require every function to include approved components, such as SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring tools. Previously, sharing these through Lambda Layers or container images meant redeploying every function to pick up a change. With customer-managed runtimes, platform teams manage these components in a central runtime, packaged as OCI container images in Amazon ECR and compatible with existing Docker and CI/CD tooling. Functions pick up updates automatically as Lambda recycles execution environments, so there's no need to redeploy each function or coordinate rollouts. Updates can be scheduled and staged to match change control policies, with centralized health metrics and rapid rollback. With this launch, the existing custom runtimes feature is renamed "bring your own language."

AWS Lambda customer-managed runtimes is now generally available in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional charge for customer-managed runtimes; functions are billed at standard Lambda rates and standard Amazon ECR pricing applies to runtime images.

To get started, build your runtime as a container image in Amazon ECR, starting from a Lambda base image or from scratch, then create a runtime, a version, and an alias. Application teams reference the runtime alias in their function configuration and keep deploying their code as .zip files. Share runtimes with other accounts or an AWS Organization by using a resource-based policy. You can create and manage customer-managed runtimes using the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, CloudFormation, or AWS CDK. To learn more, see the customer-managed runtimes documentation and launch blog post.

items.title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports audit logging
items.summary:
Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports database-internal audit logging, a fully managed capability that captures SQL statements executed on your cluster. Previously, AWS CloudTrail recorded who connected to a DSQL cluster, but not what they did once inside it. Now, financial institutions and regulated enterprises can meet production compliance requirements by capturing DDL, DML, DCL, and SELECT statements with full statement text, bind parameters, acting principal (both PostgreSQL role and AWS IAM identity), timestamp, table name, and transaction identifier.

With audit logging, you can feed SIEM systems directly from Amazon S3, satisfy auditor requirements for change accountability, and reconstruct events after security incidents. Logs are delivered as structured JSON to your S3 bucket via CloudWatch Vended Logs. Configuration requires a single SQL setting—no extension to load and no log-shipping pipeline to build.

Audit logging is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Audit logging will incur Aurora DSQL DPU charges, charges for log delivery through CloudWatch Logs, and charges for storing audit records in Amazon S3. For pricing information, see Aurora DSQL pricing. To learn more, see audit logging in the Aurora DSQL User Guide.

items.title: Amazon ElastiCache now supports distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLM inference
items.summary:
Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now offers fully managed distributed KV caching, a new capability that reduces self-hosted large language model (LLM) inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Customers who self-host LLMs pay for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can't hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. GPUs can fetch cached KV state in milliseconds to serve more requests and respond faster.

Distributed KV caching runs on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes in the same Availability Zone as the GPU fleet and connects to GPUs through Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). Distributed KV caching works with open-weight, fine-tuned, and custom models, whether they use full, sparse, hybrid, or other attention designs. You can add distributed KV caching to the inference engines you already use, including vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, through the LMCache connector with a configuration change. You can also use the open-source KVTrace tool to estimate the cost and latency reductions on your own application traffic before deploying anything, at no charge.

Distributed KV caching is available today on ElastiCache for Valkey in 13 AWS Regions across the US, Europe, and Asia Pacific. To get started, create a cluster with cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes using the AWS CLI in the same AZ as your GPU fleet and adding the endpoint to your inference engine. To learn more, read the AWS blog for a technical deep dive and performance results, or visit the Amazon ElastiCache documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon ElastiCache pricing page.

items.title: AWS Control Tower now supports existing Amazon S3 bucket for log delivery
items.summary:
AWS Control Tower now lets you use an existing Amazon S3 bucket in your landing zone to store AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail logs. Previously, AWS Control Tower required you to use the Amazon S3 bucket it creates and manages for log storage. Now, customers who want full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure can consolidate centralized logs in an Amazon S3 bucket they already manage.

You can use your own Amazon S3 bucket for both AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail, giving you full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure. You can switch between self-managed and AWS Control Tower managed buckets at any time, and your Amazon S3 buckets are preserved during landing zone updates, resets, and decommissioning. The bucket must be owned by an AWS account in your organization, be located in your AWS Control Tower home Region, and be preconfigured with the bucket policy that AWS Control Tower requires.

This feature is supported in landing zone version 4.0 and later and is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud where AWS Control Tower is available.

To learn more about configuring self-managed Amazon S3 bucket for your AWS Control Tower landing zone, visit the AWS Control Tower documentation.

items.title: AWS IAM account access manager is now even easier to deploy and use
items.summary:
Deploying and using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) account access manager is now even easier: you can use AWS managed policies to enable and administer it; you can include it in your infrastructure-as-code (IaC) configurations; and its role assignments are integrated in a growing number of third-party identity and entitlement management solutions.

Administering workforce access with account access manager requires permissions across several services, including AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS Organizations, AWS KMS, and AWS IAM. Previously, defining administrative access required hand-assembling multi-service IAM policies. The new AWS managed policies enable faster ramp up with broadly scoped job-aligned permissions for: 1/ Full administrator (AWSAccountAccessManagerAdministrator) - used to enable and manage account access manager in the AWS organization management account and to map users/groups to IAM roles; 2/ Entitlement Manager (AWSAccountAccessManagerEntitlementManager) - used to assign and remove user access without the ability to change service configuration; and 3/ ReadOnly (AWSAccountAccessManagerReadOnlyAccess) - used by auditors and compliance reviewers for visibility into user access.

Account access manager streamlines assignment of IAM roles to workforce users and groups in IAM Identity Center, bringing together access management flexibility, user awareness, and a single point of federation. You can include account access manager in your IaC configurations managed through Terraform, Pulumi, or AWS CloudFormation. The entitlements that you assign with account access manager are reflected in your identity provider (IdP) and entitlements management system, including those offered by AWS partners Okta, PingIdentity, Cisco Duo, Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai, Lumos, and SailPoint.

IAM account access manager is provided at no additional cost and available in all AWS Commercial Regions enabled by default. To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide.

items.title: Amazon S3 Replication adds exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution
items.summary:
You can now replicate data in Amazon S3 buckets with fewer replication rules using two new S3 Replication capabilities, exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution. Buckets that many tenants or applications share often need many rules to skip certain data or to match encryption keys in each AWS Region. With these capabilities, customers who manage multi-tenant and shared buckets can replace many replication rules with a single rule.

With exclusions, you can replicate an entire bucket while skipping specific prefixes or tagged objects, such as logs or experimental data. With Multi-Region key resolution, S3 Replication encrypts each replica with the matching AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Multi-Region key in the destination Region, so replicas meet the same encryption requirements as their source objects. For example, a bucket that stores data for hundreds of tenants, each with its own Multi-Region key, can replicate with a single rule, including tenants you add later.

Exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution are optional and available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions. To get started, use the AWS SDKs, AWS CLI, S3 API, or S3 console. To learn more, visit the S3 Replication product page and Replicating objects within and across Regions in the S3 User Guide.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density on EKS-orchestrated clusters
items.summary:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density per node on EKS-orchestrated clusters, allowing you to get more out of every instance. This leaves more room for your applications alongside system DaemonSets for monitoring, logging, and security, and helps increase GPU, CPU and memory utilization on nodes, allowing you to run the same work using fewer instances.

As you schedule more pods, the Amazon VPC CNI automatically adds network capacity to the node. Autoscaling with Karpenter also supports the higher pod capacity, so new nodes take on more pods as your cluster scales out.

Here are a few examples of workloads that benefit from higher pod density:

  • Model inference - Serve more model replicas or more models from each GPU instance, including on smaller types such as ml.g5 and ml.g6.

  • Interactive development - Host more notebooks, IDEs, and data science environments on each node.

  • GPU partitioning - Use all the Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) slices on instances such as ml.p5en.48xlarge, where each slice runs its own pod.

  • Operators and Controllers - Run operators, controllers, and observability agents on CPU nodes alongside your workloads, without crowding them out.

This feature is available for HyperPod EKS-orchestrated clusters in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To get started, update your cluster's IAM permissions, cluster software, and Amazon VPC CNI add-on. To learn more, please check the documentation.

items.title: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection
items.summary:
Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets.

Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in.

These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

items.title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available
items.summary:
Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale — you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user.

Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on EC2, this release adds Spark Connect support on multi-primary clusters, along with Secret Agent improvements that cut user-provisioning latency by up to 97% under high concurrency. On EMR Serverless, new scaling profiles for Spark (performance-optimized, balanced, or cost-optimized) let you tune how quickly executors scale, and applications can now run Lake Formation-governed Glue UDFs. On EMR on EKS, the Spark Operator is upgraded to version 2 (based on open-source Spark Operator 2.5.0).

Amazon EMR 8.2 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EMR 8.2 Release Guide for EMR on EC2, the EMR Serverless release notes, and the EMR on EKS release notes, or get started by creating a cluster from the Amazon EMR console.

items.title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless
items.summary:
Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. Data engineers can also use the agent during development to tune configurations before promoting to production. All access is authenticated with AWS IAM and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge in all Regions where EMR Serverless is available, except GovCloud (US) and China Regions, for EMR release versions 7.6 and later. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless.

items.title: AWS Transform now accelerates migration deals for Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) benefits
items.summary:
AWS Partners can now expedite Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) deals, from qualification to incentive payout, with an end-to-end agentic workflow in AWS Transform. Partners can manage the full MAP lifecycle without leaving AWS Transform, including deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, migration planning and execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement.

Previously, Partners had to switch between separate systems for opportunity discovery, assessments, deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. This fragmentation, along with manual handoffs between steps, led to longer qualification cycles.

Now, with the agentic MAP experience in AWS Transform, Partners connect their AWS Partner Central account and invite customers into the same engagement. Partners start by scoping customer environments with the built-in agentic discovery tool, or by importing data from RVTools or AWS-validated ISV tools listed in AWS Marketplace. AWS Transform then combines this discovery data with opportunity details from APN Customer Engagements (ACE) to automatically qualify Partner-initiated opportunities in a guided flow, so Partners get eligibility decisions sooner and close deals faster. As the migration progresses, MAP resource tags are applied automatically, and Partner cash and customer credits are disbursed based on actual usage data. Throughout, customers get shared, real-time visibility into migration projects alongside their Partner.

AWS Transform with integrated MAP is now available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) page. Partners can get started with the AWS Partner Central user guide (login required) or by contacting their Partner Development Manager. Customers can contact their AWS account team or AWS Partner.

items.title: Amazon EC2 C8gn instances are now available in AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region
items.summary:
Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8gn instances, powered by the latest-generation AWS Graviton4 processors, are available in the AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region. The C8gn instances provide up to 30% better compute performance than Graviton3-based Amazon EC2 C7gn instances. Amazon EC2 C8gn instances feature the latest 6th generation AWS Nitro Cards, and offer up to 600 Gbps network bandwidth, the highest network bandwidth among network optimized EC2 instances. 

Take advantage of the enhanced networking capabilities of C8gn to scale performance and throughput, while optimizing the cost of running network-intensive workloads such as network virtual appliances, data analytics, CPU-based artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) inference. 

For increased scalability, C8gn instances offer instance sizes up to 48xlarge, up to 384 GiB of memory, and up to 120 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS). C8gn instances support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on the 16xlarge, 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes, which enables lower latency and improved cluster performance for workloads deployed on tightly coupled clusters. 

C8gn instances are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon, N.California), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain, Zurich, Milan, Paris), Asia Pacific (Singapore, Malaysia, Sydney, Thailand, Mumbai, Seoul, Melbourne, Jakarta, Hyderabad, Tokyo, Hong Kong), Middle East (UAE), Israel (Tel Aviv), Africa (Cape Town), Canada West (Calgary, Central), South America (Sao Paulo), AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West).
 
To learn more, see Amazon C8gn Instances. To begin your Graviton journey, visit the Level up your compute with AWS Graviton page. To get started, see AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and AWS SDKs.

items.title: Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are now available in AWS Europe (Ireland) region
items.summary:
Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8ine instances are available in the AWS Europe (Ireland) region. C8ine instances are powered by custom sixth generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors, available only on AWS. These instances feature the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards, delivering up to 43% higher performance compared to previous generation C6in instances.

C8ine instances offer up to 2.5 times higher packet performance per vCPU versus prior generation network optimized instances, providing up to 2x higher network throughput for traffic going through Internet gateways compared to existing C6in network optimized instances. C8ine instances are designed for security and network virtual appliances, including virtual firewalls, load balancers, and Telco 5G UPF workloads.

Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland, Frankfurt) regions. C8ine instances are available via Savings Plans, On-Demand, and Spot instances. For more information, visit the Amazon EC2 C8i instance pages.

items.title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries
items.summary:
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition.

Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before.

Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide.

items.title: Customize AWS Elemental Inference with custom models, prompts, and decisions
items.summary:
AWS Elemental Inference now lets you customize how it analyzes your live video in two ways. You can create functions that ask custom questions of the video using multi-modal foundational models in Amazon Bedrock, or add contextual metadata decisions using labels and questions you define. Both run on the same pipeline as built-in features such as vertical video creation and smart subtitles, and return results through the GetMetadata API, with no separate pipeline to build.

Use contextual metadata decisions when the answer you need fits labels and yes/no questions. You define yes/no questions, such as whether a scene is a weather report, or "pick-one" categories, such as genre. For each scene, contextual metadata returns a decision and a confidence score for every label and question, alongside the standard Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), and mood fields, so your workflows can act when confidence meets a threshold you set. No model selection or prompt writing is required.

Use functions for open-ended answers, custom response formats, or analysis contextual metadata doesn't cover, such as sponsor logo exposure. A function specifies an Amazon Bedrock model and JSONata expressions that shape the request and response. You attach it to a feed and choose how frequently it runs.

Contextual-metadata decisions configuration is included in the contextual metadata price. Functions are available at no additional charge on feeds with at least one feature active; Amazon Bedrock usage is billed separately. Both are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental Inference is available.

To learn more, see the AWS Elemental Inference user guide.

items.title: AWS Security Hub now infers resource criticality from installed software and usage
items.summary:
Today, AWS Security Hub adds installed software and resource usage as signals for resource criticality, which indicates how important a resource is to your business. Security Hub uses criticality to rank exposure findings, so that central security teams can prioritize the exposures that affect their most important resources.

Security Hub already infers criticality from resource tags and names, but inconsistently tagged resources often have an Unknown criticality, which makes their exposures harder to prioritize. With installed software and resource usage as additional signals, more of your resources receive a meaningful criticality with no tagging or configuration required. For example, an EC2 instance that runs a database engine and serves steady traffic receives a higher criticality than an instance that runs only monitoring agents and sits idle.

These signals are included with the Security Hub Essentials plan at no additional cost and require no new enablement. To learn more, see Resources in Security Hub in the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page. For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table.

items.title: Amazon API Gateway REST APIs now support JWT authorizers
items.summary:
Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a new authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer. You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it.

You can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers.

The JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now supports short-term memory retention of up to 10 years
items.summary:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now lets you keep short-term memory events for up to 10 years, up from one year. Developers can now use short-term memory as a long-lived record of agent conversations and interactions. This helps when that history needs to stay available for a long time, such as for compliance and audit, for users who come back after months away, or for agents that need to look back at past sessions.

You set retention on the memory resource, and it's applied to each event when the event is created, so existing events keep their original retention. Standard short-term memory storage charges apply for as long as you keep the data.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is available. To get started, see the AgentCore Memory documentation.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now provides full session summaries
items.summary:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now keeps a full session summary for every session. It's a single record that gives a snapshot of what happened in the conversation. Summary chunks cover the conversation in more detail, while the full session summary captures the overall picture of where the session stands. AgentCore Memory updates it as new events arrive, so it always reflects the session so far. This works well for developers who want a quick recap rather than a play-by-play.

Full session summaries come with the summary strategy and need no extra setup. Every memory that has a summary strategy gets them automatically, including existing sessions. Each summary is stored as a long-term memory record next to the session's summary chunks. You retrieve it with the Memory operations you already use, and you can filter by record type to return only full session summaries.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is available. To get started, see the Summary strategy documentation.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker now supports AI data preparation capabilities to build high-quality datasets for model development
items.summary:
Building high-quality training datasets has traditionally required weeks of manual labeling and data cleaning. Amazon SageMaker now offers AI data preparation capabilities that help data scientists and ML engineers build high-quality training and evaluation datasets for both text-based model customization and traditional ML.

Teams can generate synthetic examples grounded in their own documents, auto-label records at scale with confidence scores, incorporate expert feedback through human review, evaluate data quality, and transform data for their chosen training or evaluation technique. Synthetic data generation creates training, evaluation, and test data from a specification grounded in your documents. Auto-labeling labels data at scale with built-in task types including classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, plus custom tasks. Rows below your confidence threshold go to a human review queue in the Label Studio Community Edition in SageMaker AI Studio. Data quality evaluation finds duplicates and surfaces issues such as tone and insufficient diversity with both quality metrics and rules. Data transformation cleans and reshapes data for your training or evaluation technique, using operators such as dedupe, filter, and format conversion.

Teams can start with just a few examples, production traces, or existing data in Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, or AWS Glue Data Catalog. Developers access these capabilities directly through the SageMaker Python SDK API or in natural language through the latest version of the AWS AI-ML skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. Your source data, generated datasets, and labels stay in your own Amazon S3 buckets, controlled by an IAM role you manage.

These capabilities are available in the US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1) and US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) regions.

To learn more, see the AI data preparation documentation.

items.title: AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Lambda Managed Instances
items.summary:
AWS Lambda now supports scale to and from zero for Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). Lambda automatically scales execution environments for your function to zero during idle periods and scales them back up when requests arrive, without requiring you to provision minimum capacity. This makes LMI cost-effective for intermittent workloads such as asynchronous processing, development, and test environments.

Lambda Managed Instances lets you run Lambda functions on your Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With Lambda Managed Instances, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing advantages, without managing infrastructure. Previously, customers needed to keep a minimum number of execution environments running even when there was no traffic. With this launch, Lambda scales execution environments for your function to zero after a period with no activity, and provisions them again when requests arrive. This improves cost efficiency for workloads with periods of no traffic.

This feature is available today in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To get started, set MinExecutionEnvironments to zero for your function using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, or AWS CDK. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

items.title: Amazon Cognito now supports authentication level and method token claims
items.summary:
Amazon Cognito now supports authentication context class reference (ACR) and authentication methods reference (AMR), by adding ACR and AMR claims to access, ID, and refresh tokens. Your application can use the authentication level (ACR) to make authorization decisions, such as requiring additional factors for sensitive operations. It can also use completed methods (AMR), such as time-based one-time password (TOTP), for auditing and compliance.

Amazon Cognito defines four authentication levels based on the factors a user completes, from password-only (level 1) to a password with a TOTP (level 4). Each token reflects the level achieved during sign-in, so your application can make authorization decisions based on how a user authenticated. If your application requires a stronger level, you can request a target level in your application's sign-in flow or through managed login, and Amazon Cognito issues new tokens once the user completes the required factors. You can also customize ACR level URIs for your user pool. For federated users from an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, Amazon Cognito maps the provider's ACR and AMR values to your levels.

ACR and AMR token claims are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is offered. Every user pool includes ACR and AMR token claims, regardless of feature plan. Requesting a target authentication level and configuring custom ACR level URIs are available with the Essentials or Plus feature plan. To get started, configure ACR and AMR using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. See developer guide for details.

items.title: Amazon DynamoDB caching is now available with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey
items.summary:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of DynamoDB caching with Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey, a serverless alternative to Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) that delivers sub-millisecond read latency for frequently accessed DynamoDB data. Previously, if you needed faster reads than the single-digit millisecond latency of DynamoDB, you had to provision and scale DAX nodes or run your own cache and keep it in sync with DynamoDB. Now you can access DynamoDB table data from a write-through cache that updates as data changes and scales automatically to meet changing workload demands, with no clusters or nodes to manage.

DynamoDB caching requires no application logic changes and minimal configuration. You choose which DynamoDB tables and APIs to cache and how long to retain cached data. Your application's IAM credentials are used to access DynamoDB, so existing access control policies are automatically applied.

DynamoDB caching is available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. DynamoDB caching is offered at no additional cost, so you pay only for the ElastiCache Serverless and DynamoDB resources your applications use. To get started, see the ElastiCache Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines
items.summary:
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports ingest pipelines, so you can clean, enrich, and vectorize documents inside your collection as they are indexed, without running separate preprocessing infrastructure. Teams building search, log analytics, and generative AI applications can replace data-prep code in Lambda functions or ETL jobs with transformations that apply consistently to every document, regardless of how it is ingested.

You can use ingest pipelines to normalize and clean data with processors such as copy, date, dot_expander, join, lowercase, uppercase, remove, rename, set, and trim. For semantic and AI search, you can chunk long text with text_chunking and generate embeddings at ingest time with text_embedding, text_image_embedding, and sparse_encoding. The ml_inference processor calls any model you have connected and lets you map its input and output fields yourself. You create and manage pipelines with the familiar OpenSearch _ingest/pipeline APIs. You can test a pipeline against sample documents with the _simulate API before sending it live traffic, then apply it as an index's default pipeline or on individual indexing and bulk requests.

Pipeline processing uses your collection's indexing OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs) and is billed the same way as other indexing activity. If you use a remote model with an ML processor, the model provider bills inference separately. Ingest pipelines are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is available.

To get started, see Ingest pipelines in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. To learn more about OpenSearch Serverless, visit the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless product page.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch UI is now available in the Africa (Cape Town) Region
items.summary:
Amazon OpenSearch UI has expanded to the AWS Africa (Cape Town) Region, bringing availability to 25 AWS Regions. OpenSearch UI provides a single endpoint to query, visualize, and analyze data across Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running OpenSearch version 1.3 or later and OpenSearch Serverless collections, including Classic and NextGen.

One OpenSearch UI application can connect to multiple domains and collections. Workspaces organize dashboards, saved queries, and other content, with purpose-built experiences for observability, security analytics, and search. The Discover interface supports multiple data sources and query languages, including Piped Processing Language (PPL) and SQL. It also includes a data selector, query autocomplete, and an updated design. OpenSearch UI runs separately from your domains and collections, giving you access to the latest UI capabilities without requiring cluster upgrades.

To get started, create an OpenSearch UI application using the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. OpenSearch UI is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the domains and collections it connects to. For the complete list of supported Regions, see OpenSearch UI endpoints and quotas. To learn more, see Using OpenSearch UI in Amazon OpenSearch Service in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion Service now supports next-generation time series collections
items.summary:
Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion service now supports time series collections in the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as a pipeline destination. You can stream logs, metrics, traces and event data into time series collections with fully managed pipelines. You don't have to run your own collectors or write custom ingestion code.

OpenSearch Ingestion delivers data from the sources you already use, including OpenTelemetry, Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK, Amazon DynamoDB, and HTTP endpoints. Before indexing, pipelines can filter, enrich, transform, and route data with built-in processors. For example, you can parse and normalize log fields, mask sensitive data, or split a stream into separate indexes. Pipelines scale automatically with your workload. Time series collections add a lower-cost warm storage tier and built-in alerting and anomaly detection. Together they give you an observability pipeline from collection to analysis with no clusters to manage.

To get started, create a pipeline in the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, through the AWS CLI, or with AWS CloudFormation, and choose a time series collection as the sink. OpenSearch Ingestion is billed in Ingestion OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs), separately from your collection. For details, see Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where both Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion and the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless are available. To get started, create a pipeline in the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, through the AWS CLI, or with AWS CloudFormation, and choose a next-generation time series collection as the sink. To learn more, see Overview of Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers free monthly web search queries
items.summary:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers 5,000 free web search queries per month through the Web Search Tool in AgentCore gateway and the Web Search API. AgentCore helps developers build, deploy, and operate highly effective agents securely at scale. Developers can now build and test agents with web search capabilities at no cost for their first 5,000 queries each month.

The free allowance applies automatically, with no setup required. It is shared across supported AWS Regions and by all accounts in an organization, and resets each month. Additional queries are billed at standard rates without interrupting your agents.

Free web search queries are available in all AWS Regions that support the Web Search Tool and Web Search API: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo).

To learn more, see AgentCore pricing, Web Search Tool in the AgentCore Developer Guide, and the AgentCore product page.

items.title: AWS Config announces managed conformance packs
items.summary:
AWS Config now offers managed conformance packs. AWS builds and maintains these packs for specific compliance and governance frameworks. When you deploy one, you choose a framework, and AWS Config evaluates your resources against it. AWS keeps the pack up to date as things change. When new AWS Config managed rules map to the framework's controls, or when the framework itself is revised, AWS updates your deployed pack automatically. Because AWS maintains a consistent pack definition in every supported Region, you can deploy the same framework across Regions without building or maintaining Region-specific rule sets. With managed conformance packs you no longer have to track framework changes or update rules yourself.

Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever new rules became available or the framework changed. Managed conformance packs remove that work, so your coverage stays current without manual template changes. Each pack includes the managed rules available in the Region where you deploy it and adds new rules as they become available there, so you don't need a separate template for each Region. You can set rule parameters to fit your environment. Compliance results and compliance scores appear in the AWS Config console alongside your other rules and conformance packs.

Managed conformance packs cover frameworks including PCI DSS v4, SOC 2, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and CIS Controls, along with AI governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF 1.0. For the full list, see the AWS Config documentation page.

Managed conformance packs are available in all AWS commercial Regions except Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For the full list of supported Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. Evaluations are billed at standard conformance pack evaluation rates. To get started, open the AWS Config console and choose Conformance packs. To learn more, see the AWS Config Developer Guide and the AWS Config pricing page.

items.title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now offers SQL statement statistics in Database Insights
items.summary:
Amazon Aurora DSQL now records statistics for each SQL statement your cluster runs and publishes them as Amazon CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics. You can view them in Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights. For each statement, you see how often it runs, how long it takes, the rows it scans, returns, or changes, and the DPUs it uses.

Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity. Use them to find the statements that take the most time, run most often, or cost the most. In Database Insights, choose a statement under Top SQL to see its normalized SQL text and per-call charts. You can also query the metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch. Turn on statement statistics for each cluster in the Aurora DSQL console or the API when you create or update the cluster.

Statement statistics are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Standard CloudWatch metrics and Logs charges apply, with no additional Aurora DSQL charge. To learn more, see monitoring SQL statements with statement statistics in the Aurora DSQL User Guide and CloudWatch pricing.

items.title: Amazon EVS launches support for r7i.metal instances, external principal storage, and an Agent Skill
items.summary:
Today, we are announcing that Amazon Elastic VMware Service (Amazon EVS) now supports the r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) bare metal instance types for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.x deployments. EC2 r7i instances are memory optimized, with custom 4th Generation Intel Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids) processors, and designed to be used with external storage. With these instances possessing no local NVMe disks, Amazon EVS now supports VCF external principal storage with solutions such as Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. With this launch, you can use the Amazon EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) within the Solutions for EVS GitHub repository to fully automate the end-to-end deployment and configuration of your VCF 9.x environment on EVS.

With this release, you now have more options for running VMware-based Virtual Machines (VM) in your Amazon VPC - while keeping the same tools, skills, and operational processes, and full control of your architecture, configuration, and lifecycle of your environment. 

We are also launching a new Amazon EVS Agent Skill, which gives your AI Agents context to help you plan, deploy, and operate your Amazon EVS environments - from answering questions and recommending designs to generating blueprints and driving deployments with EDO. To get started, point the AI agent of your choice to the EVS Agent Skill file in the latest release of the EVS GitHub repository.  

This release is available in all regions where Amazon EVS is offered. To learn more about Amazon EVS, visit the product detail page and the user guide.

items.title: OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Sol are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6.2 Astra brings frontier-level reasoning and judgment to your most ambitious work, including complex business problems, demanding research, and advanced coding and agentic workflows. Astra also includes an Ultrafast mode for latency-sensitive applications that need fast responses. GPT-6.2 Sol is designed for recurring coding, agentic, and professional workflows with clear outcomes, where speed and cost per task matter.

Use GPT-6.2 Astra for challenging work that calls for expert judgment and a finished deliverable, such as reconciling competing inputs, investigating complex codebases, reasoning across text and images, and creating professional artifacts. Select ultrafast mode for Astra for interactive coding assistants, real-time agents, and customer-facing applications where latency shapes the customer experience. Use GPT-6.2 Sol for recurring, high-volume work with verifiable outcomes, such as implementing and debugging software, analyzing documents and data, and automating multistep workflows. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. 

You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

items.title: Amazon VPC, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN now offer a 99.999% availability SLA for cross-Region traffic
items.summary:
AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a new capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming.

The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the issue in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. Some applications, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming, can't tolerate single-digit seconds interruptions, let alone minutes of unavailability. Until now, customers running these applications relied on workarounds, including modifying their applications and operating systems to split a single connection into multiple connections, or replicating data into every Region to avoid cross-Region calls. These workarounds add complexity and don't always work, because applications can't control which network paths their traffic takes.

Now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths. It delivers whichever copy reaches your resources in the destination Region first and discards the duplicates. If one path drops packets, a copy is already in flight on another path, so your applications stay connected without waiting for the network protocols to reroute. Multipath Resilience moves this work out of your applications and into the network. Your applications keep using a single connection, with no changes to application code or operating systems, and no need to duplicate data to keep calls within a single Region.

Multipath Resilience is now generally available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the Multipath Resilience documentation. For SLA details, visit the Multipath Resilience SLA. For pricing, visit the Amazon VPC pricing page.

items.title: Amazon MSK Standard Brokers now support Graviton4-based M8g instances
items.summary:
AWS Graviton4-based M8g instances are now generally available for Standard Brokers in Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). Compared to Standard Brokers on M7g, M8g delivers up to 35% lower P99 produce latency and 30% faster catch-up for consumers that fall behind.

Standard Brokers on M8g are available today across all AWS regions where MSK Standard Brokers and M8g instances are available. For pricing, refer to the Amazon MSK pricing page. To get started, use the AWS Management Console or API to create a new cluster with Standard Brokers on M8g or start an in-place migration of an existing cluster from Standard Brokers on M7g to M8g. To learn more, see the Amazon MSK Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS announces general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud connectivity with Microsoft Azure
items.summary:
AWS announces the general availability of AWS Interconnect - multicloud with Microsoft Azure.

Customers have been adopting multicloud strategies while migrating more applications to the cloud. They do so for many reasons including interoperability requirements, the freedom to choose technology that best suits their needs, and the ability to build and deploy applications on any environment with greater ease and speed. Previously, when interconnecting workloads across multiple cloud providers (CSPs), customers had to go the route of a ‘do-it-yourself’ multicloud approach, leading to complexities of building and managing global multi-layered networks at scale. AWS Interconnect - multicloud is the first purpose-built product of its kind and a new way of how clouds connect and talk to each other, allowing customers to quickly provision resilient, scalable private connections to other cloud providers.

In August, Microsoft Azure launched support for AWS Interconnect in public preview and became the latest CSP to adopt the open specification that powers the service. With today’s GA launch, AWS customers can now rely on the same consistent, simple experience to interconnect their workloads on Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

Interconnect - multicloud is available with Microsoft Azure in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia), ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), and eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Regions. You can create an Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - multicloud documentation.

items.title: Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience
items.summary:
Amazon WorkSpaces provides a new Windows client experience for Amazon WorkSpaces Personal.
